title: UX trends for 2027: less interface, more responsibility
summary: The UX shifts to prepare for in 2027, from conversational interfaces and AI actions to accessibility, better research and responsibility for the whole service.
body_markdown:
The easiest UX prediction for 2027 is that everything will have AI in it.


The more useful question is whether any of it will make the experience better.


Adding a conversational interface to a confusing service does not resolve the confusion. Generating more screens does not establish which ones people need. Automating a process does not make its decisions sensible.


Our view is that the most important UX developments in 2027 will concern what happens beyond the screen: how people express what they need, how systems act on it, and how organisations take responsibility for the result.


These are the shifts we would prepare for.


## 1. Conversation will become part of the interface, but it should earn its place


[Conversational interfaces](https://www.thisisabsurd.com/blog/designing-for-chatbots) offer an appealing starting point: describe what you want instead of learning how an organisation has arranged its navigation.


That is useful when the need is complicated.


“Find somewhere we can stay with two children, arriving on Friday, with an accessible room” contains several requirements that a conventional journey might spread across filters, forms and separate pages.


But conversation is a poor replacement for every interaction.


Choosing a date from a calendar can be easier than explaining it. Comparing three options side by side can be clearer than reading three paragraphs. A visible button can be more discoverable than an undocumented capability.


We expect the stronger experiences in 2027 to combine conversation with familiar controls. People should be able to explain, compare, select and edit in whichever way suits the task.


A chat box should remove work, not give people another interface to negotiate.


## 2. Designing for AI actions will matter more than designing AI answers


AI systems can already use tools and interact with websites. That changes the design problem.


An answer can be wrong. An action can change a booking, send information or spend money.


The interface needs to make the difference obvious.


What is the system proposing? What has it actually done? Which information did it use? Where does it need permission? What happens if it only completes half the task?


Those questions deserve as much design attention as the initial request.


Our prediction is that review screens, clear permissions, progress states and recovery journeys will become defining features of good AI experiences.


A reassuring tone is insufficient. People need practical control.


The most important moment may be the one just before the system commits.


## 3. Brand experience will extend into interfaces you do not own


Organisations have spent years refining the experience on their own websites.


An assistant acting on somebody’s behalf introduces another route. It might interpret product information, compare services or attempt to complete a task without following the journey your team carefully designed.


We would not predict the disappearance of websites. We would question the assumption that every customer will experience your carefully arranged homepage.


That makes accurate content, explicit pricing, useful product attributes and[dependable service connections](https://www.thisisabsurd.com/blog/what-is-mcp-for-organisations) part of the UX brief.


Consider an appointment service. A beautifully designed treatment page cannot compensate for availability that is impossible to establish or referral requirements that only emerge after an enquiry.


Preparing for these journeys starts with making the offer understandable and actionable.


Your brand is also represented by the accuracy of the information somebody else retrieves.


## 4. Accessibility will expose the weaknesses in adaptive interfaces


An interface that changes in response to a request sounds helpful.


It also raises difficult questions.


Does keyboard focus move somewhere sensible when new controls appear? Does a screen reader announce the result? Can someone revisit a previous decision? Are labels and navigation still predictable?


These are design requirements, not details to resolve after the exciting part is finished.


Existing accessibility guidance already addresses issues such as obscured focus, repeated information entry and accessible authentication. More dynamic interfaces give teams additional places to get those fundamentals wrong.


For 2027, we would prioritise[accessible components and interaction rules](https://www.thisisabsurd.com/blog/from-guidelines-to-systems-why-design-systems-are-now-essential) that remain dependable when content or layouts change.


An interface should not become harder to use because it is trying to be clever.


## 5. Faster prototyping will put more pressure on the quality of the question


AI can help teams produce working ideas quickly. That makes experimentation attractive.


It does not tell you whether the idea addresses a worthwhile problem.


Ten convincing prototypes can still represent ten versions of the wrong assumption. A generated persona cannot tell you what an actual customer experienced yesterday.


We expect the useful shift to be shorter cycles between a specific question, a functioning prototype and[observation of real people using it](https://www.thisisabsurd.com/blog/user-testing-and-how-we-deploy-it-at-absurd) .


That requires judgement about what to investigate. It also requires teams to abandon ideas when the evidence fails to support them.


Research should influence a decision. Prototypes should test an uncertainty.


The advantage is learning sooner, not producing more things to review.


## 6. UX will need to account for the work it creates elsewhere


A journey can look successful in analytics while transferring effort to another part of the organisation.


An enquiry form gets completed, but the information is insufficient to act on. A chatbot resolves a conversation, but the customer contacts support again. A booking converts, but unclear conditions lead to a cancellation.


We would push[UX measurement further into the service](https://www.thisisabsurd.com/service-design) .


Alongside conversion, examine repeat contact, failed handovers, correction work and whether people actually complete what they set out to do.


The right measures depend on the organisation. A private hospital, a retailer and a membership organisation should not share a generic definition of success.


For 2027, our position is straightforward: a better interface should produce a better outcome for the customer and a service the organisation can reliably deliver.


If the screen improves while the problem moves elsewhere, the design is unfinished.


## What should organisations do now?


Choose an important customer journey. Identify where people struggle, where staff compensate and where information becomes unreliable.


Then establish which changes would improve the outcome. Some may involve AI. Others may involve clearer content, fewer steps or a better connection between existing systems.


The most useful[UX investment for 2027](https://www.thisisabsurd.com/services/digital-strategy) will be the one that makes a difficult task easier to complete, with enough clarity and control for people to trust the result.
